experiment.title: LCOR DNA binding HTH domain, Psq-type from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the LCOR DNA binding HTH domain, Psq-type from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the DNA binding HTH domain, Psq-type in LCOR using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q96JN0_PF05225_353.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the PDZ domain in MAGI2 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q86UL8_PF00595_601.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

scoreSets.title: MRTFA SAP domain domainome 1.0
scoreSets.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the MRTFA SAP domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: MRTFA SAP domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the MRTFA SAP domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the SAP domain in MRTFA using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q969V6_PF02037_341.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).
